scene-u01-pnew1-81.text: can one network give the effect of averaging many?

scene-u01-pnew1-83.name: text#83
scene-u01-pnew1-83.text: Train one, get the benefit of averaging many.

scene-u01-pnew2-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew2-25.text: Dropout: switch off a random part of the neurons at every step

scene-u01-pnew2-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew2-26.text: Each neuron is independently kept with probability $p$ and switched off (output $0$) with probability $1-p$.

scene-u01-pnew2-65.name: text#65
scene-u01-pnew2-65.text: under one mask: two hidden neurons switched off

scene-u01-pnew2-96.name: text#96
scene-u01-pnew2-96.text: mask $\mathbf m=(m_1,\dots,m_n)$; the layer output becomes $\mathbf m\odot\mathbf h$; $m_i=1$ kept, $m_i=0$ off.

scene-u01-pnew2-98.name: text#98
scene-u01-pnew2-98.text: The next step draws a new mask; the crosses move.

scene-u01-pnew2-100.name: text#100
scene-u01-pnew2-100.text: Each step's forward and backward pass use only the kept neurons.

scene-u01-pnew3-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew3-26.text: Each neuron is switched off independently, so there are $2^n$ masks.

scene-u01-pnew3-182.name: text#182
scene-u01-pnew3-182.text:
a layer of $1000$ neurons: about $10^{301}$
(far more than the atoms in the universe)

scene-u01-pnew3-184.name: text#184
scene-u01-pnew3-184.text: Analogy: each practice a few random players are absent. There are $2^n$ line-ups, yet everyone drills the same playbook: all sub-networks share one set of weights.

scene-u01-pnew3-186.name: text#186
scene-u01-pnew3-186.text: Each step draws one mask = one line-up updated once; most never play, but sharing the playbook they benefit too.

scene-u01-pnew3-188.name: text#188
scene-u01-pnew3-188.text: Dropout = cheap model averaging: train a huge crowd of weight-sharing sub-networks.

scene-u01-pnew4-25.text: Why scale at test time: in training the input averages only $p$ times the full one

orange: each present half

scene-u01-pnew4-48.text: This uses the linearity of expectation.

scene-u01-pnew4-50.name: text#50
scene-u01-pnew4-50.text: Analogy: four taps, each open half the time: the average flow is half of fully open. At test time all are open, so there is more water than in training; multiply by $p$.

scene-u01-pnew4-52.name: text#52
scene-u01-pnew4-52.text: Weight scaling: at test time multiply this layer's output (or the next layer's weights) by $p$.

scene-u01-pnew5-72.text: Analogy: $16$ absence line-ups each play one match; single scores swing (this one $4$ vs full $2$): one draw is noisy, the average is accurate.

scene-u01-pnew6-74.text: Using the full network at test time gives an input twice the training average.

scene-u01-pnew7-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew7-25.text: Today's way: divide by $p$ during training (inverted dropout)

scene-u01-pnew7-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew7-26.text: Move the scaling to the training side; nothing changes at test time.

scene-u01-pnew7-44.name: text#44
scene-u01-pnew7-44.text: e.g. $\mathbf h=(2,-1,3,1)$: the mean output is exactly $\mathbf h$.

scene-u01-pnew7-46.name: text#46
scene-u01-pnew7-46.text: Analogy: a microphone muted half the time, doubled when on: average loudness unchanged. At test time use the full network; deployment need not remember to multiply by $p$.

scene-u01-pnew7-48.name: text#48
scene-u01-pnew7-48.text: Both are equivalent in expectation; the scaling just moves to training.

scene-u01-pnew8-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew8-25.text: The scaled output only approximates the sub-network average

scene-u01-pnew8-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew8-26.text: Simplest example: $1$ neuron, $p=0.5$, output scores $(2m,\,0)$ ($m\in\{0,1\}$ is the mask).

scene-u01-pnew8-58.name: text#58
scene-u01-pnew8-58.text: Analogy: setting the volume midway between two singers is not the same as the average of their duet. In practice the approximation works well (added: Srivastava et al. 2014), but that is experience, not a theorem.

scene-u01-pnew8-60.name: text#60
scene-u01-pnew8-60.text: A good approximation, not the exact average.

scene-u01-pnew9-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew9-25.text: How it differs from "train $k$ independent models and average"

scene-u01-pnew9-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew9-26.text: Shared weights: cheap, but the sub-networks are not independent.

scene-u01-pnew9-28.name: text#28
scene-u01-pnew9-28.text: $k$ independent models: each its own playbook

scene-u01-pnew9-132.name: text#132
scene-u01-pnew9-132.text: trained separately on different data or initial values

scene-u01-pnew9-133.name: text#133

scene-u01-pnew9-141.name: text#141
scene-u01-pnew9-141.text: about $1$ time (a bit slower to converge)

scene-u01-pnew9-152.name: text#152
scene-u01-pnew9-152.text: Benefit: cheap. Price: line-ups share one playbook, so they are not independent and cancel errors less than truly independent teams.

scene-u01-pnew9-154.name: text#154
scene-u01-pnew9-154.text: Shared weights bring cheapness and "not independent enough".

scene-u01-pnew10-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew10-25.text: Using it in PyTorch: three points

scene-u01-pnew10-26.name: text#26

scene-u01-pnew10-34.name: text#34
scene-u01-pnew10-34.text: The opposite of this unit's keep probability. At $p=0.5$ they coincide and are easily confused; $0.8$ drops $80\%$, it does not keep it.

scene-u01-pnew10-51.name: text#51
scene-u01-pnew10-51.text: model.train() before training, always model.eval() before evaluation.

scene-u01-pnew10-52.name: text#52
scene-u01-pnew10-52.text: Forgetting eval() keeps switching neurons off: results differ every call and are worse.

scene-u01-pnew10-62.name: text#62
scene-u01-pnew10-62.text: PyTorch divides the kept outputs by $p$ during training, so there is nothing to multiply at test time.

scene-u01-pnew10-64.name: text#64
scene-u01-pnew10-64.text: nn.Dropout(p=1.0 - keep_prob): convert keep probability to drop probability.

scene-u01-pnew10-66.name: text#66
scene-u01-pnew10-66.text: Remember: drop probability, train/eval, no extra multiply by $p$.

scene-u01-pnew11-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew11-25.text: Rules of thumb, and four common misconceptions

scene-u01-pnew11-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew11-26.text: Added: rules of thumb are common practice, not theorems.

scene-u01-pnew11-36.name: text#36
scene-u01-pnew11-36.text: Fewer neurons per update: slower convergence, often more epochs; not needed when the model is small and does not overfit.

scene-u01-pnew11-42.name: text#42
scene-u01-pnew11-42.text: the goal is non-dependent neurons and a steadier whole.

scene-u01-pnew11-65.name: text#65
scene-u01-pnew11-65.text: "Switch neurons off at test time too"

scene-u01-pnew11-66.name: text#66
scene-u01-pnew11-66.text: No: everything on at test time.

scene-u01-pnew11-100.name: text#100
scene-u01-pnew11-100.text: No: sub-networks share weights and are not independent.

steps.label: KP11 · 1/11
steps.speakerNotes: KP05 said an overfit model is too flexible and too sensitive to the details of the training data. The four coloured curves are four models fitted on different noisy data, each wiggling its own way; the grey dashed line is the true pattern. (Fixed-seed illustration, computed in code.)

steps.label: KP11 · 1/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: KP05 said an overfit model is too flexible and too sensitive to the details of the training data. The four coloured curves are four models fitted on different noisy data, each wiggling its own way; the grey dashed line is the true pattern. (Fixed-seed illustration, computed in code.)

steps.label: KP11 · 1/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Averaging (thick green line) lets errors in different directions cancel: the four models' mean error is 0.075, after averaging 0.025. The problem: even one deep network is expensive to train, and many are out of reach.

steps.label: KP11 · 1/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Can we train a single network and still get the effect of averaging many models? That is the question dropout answers.

steps.label: KP11 · 2/11
steps.speakerNotes: Left: the ordinary full network, every line carries a weight.

steps.label: KP11 · 2/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Left: the ordinary full network, every line carries a weight.

steps.label: KP11 · 2/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Right: the same weights under one mask: two hidden neurons are crossed and all lines attached to them vanish, leaving a smaller network.

steps.label: KP11 · 2/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Under mask m the layer output becomes m ⊙ h (element-wise); each entry of m is independently 1 with probability p. Forward and backward passes of this step use only the kept neurons; the next step draws a new mask. Here p is the keep probability.

steps.label: KP11 · 3/11
steps.speakerNotes: n = 4 gives 2⁴ = 16 masks; n = 100 gives 2¹⁰⁰ ≈ 1.27 × 10³⁰; a layer of 1000 neurons about 10³⁰¹. (Computed in code.)

steps.label: KP11 · 3/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: n = 4 gives 2⁴ = 16 masks; n = 100 gives 2¹⁰⁰ ≈ 1.27 × 10³⁰; a layer of 1000 neurons about 10³⁰¹. (Computed in code.)

steps.label: KP11 · 3/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: All sub-networks share one set of weights: a neuron's weights are the same numbers in every sub-network that keeps it, and are updated each time it is kept. (Analogy: each practice a few random players are absent; 2ⁿ line-ups, one playbook; the 16 small cards on the left are all masks for n = 4.)

steps.label: KP11 · 3/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Each training step draws one mask, i.e. picks one sub-network and updates it once. There are far too many to train each; one run visits a tiny fraction and most are never drawn; it works because weights are shared. That is why dropout is called cheap model averaging.

steps.label: KP11 · 4/11
steps.speakerNotes: In training each neuron is present only with probability p. Take the input z = wᵀh of a linear unit in the next layer; under a mask it is z_m = Σ wᵢ mᵢ hᵢ. The expectation of mᵢ is p. Blue bars are the contributions wᵢhᵢ = (2, −2, 3, −1) of the full network, total z = 2.

steps.label: KP11 · 4/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: In training each neuron is present only with probability p. Take the input z = wᵀh of a linear unit in the next layer; under a mask it is z_m = Σ wᵢ mᵢ hᵢ. The expectation of mᵢ is p. Blue bars are the contributions wᵢhᵢ = (2, −2, 3, −1) of the full network, total z = 2.

steps.label: KP11 · 4/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Orange bars are each neuron's average contribution when present half the time (half height), total 1 = p z. By linearity of expectation: E(z_m) = Σ wᵢ E(mᵢ) hᵢ = p Σ wᵢ hᵢ = p z. (Bar heights computed from h and w.)

steps.label: KP11 · 4/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Analogy: four taps, each open half the time: the average flow is half of fully open. With everything on at test time the input would exceed the training average, so multiply by p: this layer's output, or the next layer's weights; the weight scaling rule.

steps.label: KP11 · 5/11
steps.speakerNotes: Full input z = 1·2 + 2·(−1) + 1·3 + (−1)·1 = 2. Mask (1, 0, 1, 1), second neuron off: z_m = 2 + 0 + 3 − 1 = 4, larger than the full 2; one mask can deviate a lot.

steps.label: KP11 · 5/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Full input z = 1·2 + 2·(−1) + 1·3 + (−1)·1 = 2. Mask (1, 0, 1, 1), second neuron off: z_m = 2 + 0 + 3 − 1 = 4, larger than the full 2; one mask can deviate a lot.

steps.label: KP11 · 5/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: All 16 masks each occur with probability 1/16; the 16 values are −3, −2, −1, −1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5. (Enumerated in code.)

steps.label: KP11 · 5/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Their mean is 1.0 = p z = 0.5 × 2, exactly. The std is 2.1213, matching √(p(1−p) Σ(wᵢhᵢ)²) = √(0.25 × 18): one mask is noisy, the average is accurate. (Analogy: 16 absence line-ups each play one match, single scores swing, the average is accurate. Each square is one mask; histogram enumerated in code.)

steps.label: KP11 · 6/11
steps.speakerNotes: Take h and w of 20 neurons (fixed seed 23), p = 0.5, draw 20000 masks. The blue histogram is these 20000 inputs, bell-shaped: the sub-networks each say something different. (Re-run in code with the lecture's seed; bin width 0.5.)

steps.label: KP11 · 6/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Take h and w of 20 neurons (fixed seed 23), p = 0.5, draw 20000 masks. The blue histogram is these 20000 inputs, bell-shaped: the sub-networks each say something different. (Re-run in code with the lecture's seed; bin width 0.5.)

steps.label: KP11 · 6/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The green line is p z = 1.852 at the centre; the mean over masks is 1.8340 with std 2.0989, close to p z; the gap is sampling error.

steps.label: KP11 · 6/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The dashed red line is the full network's z = 3.704, right of the centre. Using the full network at test time gives an input twice the training average, hence multiply by p.

steps.label: KP11 · 7/11
steps.speakerNotes: Almost every library today does not scale at test time but divides the kept neurons' outputs by p during training, i.e. uses (1/p) m ⊙ h. (Added.) Left: one neuron with h = 3: present half the time it outputs (1/p) h = 6; absent half the time it outputs 0.

steps.label: KP11 · 7/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Almost every library today does not scale at test time but divides the kept neurons' outputs by p during training, i.e. uses (1/p) m ⊙ h. (Added.) Left: one neuron with h = 3: present half the time it outputs (1/p) h = 6; absent half the time it outputs 0.

steps.label: KP11 · 7/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Mean = ½ × 6 + ½ × 0 = 3 = h. I.e. E((1/p) mᵢ hᵢ) = (1/p) p hᵢ = hᵢ; checking h = (2, −1, 3, 1) term by term, the mean = h.

steps.label: KP11 · 7/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Analogy: a microphone muted half the time, doubled when on: average loudness unchanged. At test time use the full network unchanged. The two ways are equivalent in expectation; the scaling just moves to training so deployment need not remember to multiply by p.

steps.label: KP11 · 8/11
steps.speakerNotes: Simplest example: one neuron, keep probability 0.5, two output scores (2m, 0), m the mask. The curve is the sigmoid σ(s): for m = 1, s = 2 and the class-1 probability is σ(2) = 0.8808; for m = 0, s = 0, σ(0) = 0.5.

steps.label: KP11 · 8/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Simplest example: one neuron, keep probability 0.5, two output scores (2m, 0), m the mask. The curve is the sigmoid σ(s): for m = 1, s = 2 and the class-1 probability is σ(2) = 0.8808; for m = 0, s = 0, σ(0) = 0.5.

steps.label: KP11 · 8/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The average of the two sub-network predictions is (0.8808 + 0.5)/2 ≈ 0.6904, the midpoint of the chord between the two points.

steps.label: KP11 · 8/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The scaled prediction replaces m by p = 0.5, i.e. s = 1, giving σ(1) ≈ 0.7311, on the curve and different from 0.6904. So the scaled output approximates the sub-network average, not the exact arithmetic mean. Mathematically scaling corresponds to a normalized geometric mean; not proved here. In practice it works well, but that is experience, not a theorem. (Curve and numbers checked in code.)

steps.label: KP11 · 9/11
steps.speakerNotes: Compare independent training of k models with dropout. Where the models come from: separately trained on different data or initial values vs. one data set with random masks picking sub-networks. Between models: independent weights vs. shared weights.

steps.label: KP11 · 9/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Compare independent training of k models with dropout. Where the models come from: separately trained on different data or initial values vs. one data set with random masks picking sub-networks. Between models: independent weights vs. shared weights.

steps.label: KP11 · 9/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Training cost: k times vs. about 1 time (slower convergence). Prediction cost: run k models and average vs. 1 pass. What is averaged: arithmetic mean or majority vote vs. scaling approximating the sub-network average.

steps.label: KP11 · 9/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Shared weights give two results: cheap; but the sub-networks are not independent, so errors cancel less than for truly independent models. A useful intuition: dropout forces every neuron not to rely on a particular partner being present, so it must learn features useful in many combinations, like letting only some players practise each time so each can stand alone.

steps.label: KP11 · 10/11
steps.speakerNotes: Compare independent training of k models with dropout. Top: left, three networks each with its own playbook (independent weights); right, one network rotating line-ups on one shared playbook. Point 1: the p of nn.Dropout(p=...) is the drop probability, the opposite of this unit's keep probability; at nn.Dropout(p=0.5) both are 0.5 and easily confused, but with 0.8 the mistake shows.

steps.label: KP11 · 10/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Compare independent training of k models with dropout. Top: left, three networks each with its own playbook (independent weights); right, one network rotating line-ups on one shared playbook. Point 1: the p of nn.Dropout(p=...) is the drop probability, the opposite of this unit's keep probability; at nn.Dropout(p=0.5) both are 0.5 and easily confused, but with 0.8 the mistake shows.

steps.label: KP11 · 10/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Point 2: call model.train() before training and always model.eval() before evaluation; forgetting eval() keeps switching neurons off at test time, so results differ on every call and are worse.

steps.label: KP11 · 10/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Point 3: PyTorch uses inverted dropout, so nothing is multiplied by p at test time. The conversion is nn.Dropout(p=1.0 − keep_prob). Note: the lecture's example code was not run in this environment, only its logic cross-checked with numpy.

steps.label: KP11 · 11/11
steps.speakerNotes: Rules of thumb (added, common practice): hidden-layer keep probability often 0.5, the input layer a larger 0.8 to 0.9 since losing an input loses information. Dropout makes each update use fewer neurons, so convergence is usually slower and often needs more epochs; not needed when the model is small and does not overfit.

steps.label: KP11 · 11/11 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Rules of thumb (added, common practice): hidden-layer keep probability often 0.5, the input layer a larger 0.8 to 0.9 since losing an input loses information. Dropout makes each update use fewer neurons, so convergence is usually slower and often needs more epochs; not needed when the model is small and does not overfit.

steps.label: KP11 · 11/11 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Four misconceptions: dropout makes the network weaker (the goal is non-dependent neurons and a steadier whole); switch neurons off at test time too (no, everything on); nn.Dropout(p=0.8) keeps 80% (wrong, it drops 80%); dropout is independent models averaged (no, sub-networks share weights and are not independent).

steps.label: KP11 · 11/11 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: One last question for KP12: dropout changes the network's structure at random during training. Another family changes the distribution of each layer's input: the input of each layer changes with the weights of earlier layers and training becomes unstable. Can we steady the input directly between layers? That is what KP12, batch normalization, answers.
